title: Publishing question
author: IhorFilonenko
selftext:
Hi there, 

I want to publish my game on steam as a solo developer. Are there any caveats for

comments.author: Square-Yam-3772
comments.body:
Sure, I have 2 ai games on steam. What kind of caveat do you have in mind? 

I guess the obvious one is that it costs money and you can lose money if nobody ended up buying your game...

replies.author: IhorFilonenko
replies.body: No, I don’t worry about money. The question is, are there any Steam publishing regulations about having ai incorporated in the project.

replies.author: Square-Yam-3772
replies.body: Yes. You just follow their policy and that's it. You can do your research about it

replies.author: IhorFilonenko
replies.body: If they cancel publication for whatever reason do  they refund money? Or I should post it again. I’m not trying anything sneaky I swear, just curious how that works

replies.author: Square-Yam-3772
replies.body: I have no idea since my games aren't canceled. You will have to look into the specific of steam policy and guidelines. They got online documentation

replies.author: IhorFilonenko
replies.body: Thank you very much. I hope your games doing well.

comments.author: derAres
comments.body:
asked claude for you.

**The one thing you must do:** Check some boxes in Steam's publishing form saying where you used AI — like if AI made your artwork, music, writing, or generates stuff while the player is playing.

**What you don't need to disclose:** Using AI to help you *code* or speed up your workflow behind the scenes. That doesn't count.

comments.author: ffxivthrowaway03
comments.body:
Licensing is the big one.  Just because something is AI-generated does not mean it's CC0 licensed.  Depending on what tool you used to generate something, if it was a service or locally run, the terms of the underlying model, etc, you could be in violation of those licensing terms without attribution or just for commercial use in general.  

Is anyone likely to catch you and care?  Probably not, but if a game gets popular enough you could be sitting on a legal landmine.

replies.author: IhorFilonenko
replies.body: I suppose only art needs licensing (and music if it generated).

replies.author: ffxivthrowaway03
replies.body: Don't forget the traditional licensing pitfalls too- fonts, premade assets you may have downloaded from asset packs, SFX packs, middleware or premade code libraries, etc.  It's a real pain to keep track of it all.

replies.author: IhorFilonenko
replies.body: That sounds as a real pain. What happens when I accidentally forget about something? Do they ban my game forever or it’s gonna be suspended until I change or update licensing?

replies.author: ffxivthrowaway03
replies.body:
Realistically?  Nothing.  The platform (steam, gog, etc) don't outright care as *they* are not the license holder of the thing you violated.  

The people who own the rights to the font, or the image, or whatever would first need to *notice* you did it, then need to come after you for infringement - at which point (at least speaking for the US) it's a civil legal matter.  They may get a temporary injunction that they *do* pass along to platforms, halting further sales of your game until the legal issue is resolved (most likely outcome is a settlement where they charge you a comparatively silly amount of money and extend you rights to keep using it).

**That being said**: What's the real risk? It depends on the infringement.  A font?  Someone might notice the font matches another font, but the actual person who made the font?  Not likely gonna ever know your game even exists.  As long as you don't like, reuse Apple's San Francisco font, it's likely nobody's gonna notice or care if you misattributed a font.  Art assets and music tend to be more noticeable, especially if you reuse something from a big product - I recognized immediately that LogMeIn's customer support hold music was straight ripped from Chrono Trigger (and they likely still got away with it, because Square Enix Legal likely was not calling LogMeIn's customer support in 2013).

For specifically generative AI works - that's where it gets even trickier.  Yes, the model might require attribution per it's licensing or say no commercial use.  But we *cant even reliably identify generative AI* at this point, much less which specific model created something.  I'm not saying don't worry about it, but unless the outputs are being tagged with some kind of metadata in the background that survives being imported into your project... the model owners are not feasibly going to be able to assert that it was *their* model that generated *your* assets and you're in breach of their licensing agreement.

As a truly solo publisher just pushing your projects to Steam, as long as you're not blatantly ripping anyone off it's really not a major risk, just something to be mindful of.  It's more an issue if you decide to take your project to an actual publisher - you need to be able to show them that your licensing is in order because *they* don't want to take on unnecessary risk that they're gonna get sued because you copy/pasted Apple's fonts.

replies.author: IhorFilonenko
replies.body: I appreciate the cohesive answer. Honestly, I am not planning on blatantly using somebody else’s assets (and haven’t used before). However, as it’s my first project, it’s better to aware than having to deal with consequences. Anyway, thank you very much for

replies.author: samuele_v
replies.body: If it helps, ask your coding AI assistant (if you use one) to keep track of all external (AI or otherwise) assets in a CREDITS.md file and to update it everytime you insert a new asset into the project. Most services have paid plans that allow for commercial usage, but many free tiers (e.g. Meshy's free tier) do NOT allow commercial usage. Some assets require attribution, some do not and it's just courtesy. Things like RemoveBG need a paid plan for commercial usage even though realistically no one would notice (but I like to keep everything clean and upfront). A full sweep shouldn't take more than an hour or so!

replies.author: IhorFilonenko
replies.body: Yeah, I was thinking about just double checking it. Thank you for advice
